plan:zero.thesis: Machines can now do thinking work cheaply, even on a home computer, and that ends the old deal of selling your days so you can eat. In this book the Singularity is the point where intelligence stops being scarce, and the institutions built on that scarcity start failing before anyone has written their replacement. CT forecasts AGI by Thanksgiving 2027, names what would prove him wrong, and shows that every step he asks for still holds if he is wrong. The danger is the people and the arrangements around the machine, not the machine itself: our ability to produce and our security can move in opposite directions, and a gain in what we can make should become a gain in how we can live. There is already enough food. Hunger, eviction and credit gatekeeping are rules people enforce, and rules can change. So we start with food. We use the machines, and the people who already do this work, to make adequate food available to everyone regardless of income or employment. Then come land, shelter and care, owned close to home by the people who depend on them, with money made optional rather than abolished. The machine is new, but the human stampede around it has happened before. A reader who starts with nothing should finish knowing what is happening, why it matters to them, and what to do this week, this year, and at the next public meeting.

spine.idea: The robots have won the old deal: what you lose is having to sell your days to eat, and that loss is an opening (CT's 2024 first line and its turn).
What is happening: thought itself is automated, cheap and local. This is a tool that can make tools, which nothing before it could.
Go around the pundits and the author and use the tools yourself.
Surviving the Singularity means keeping people fed, housed and cared for, and having a say in who owns the tools. Grow our food first.
The second ox: AI is a thinking draft animal that people must train, feed and direct. The plow doesn't pull itself.
Fired on a Tuesday, but dinner is already handled: what it looks like if it goes right.
Listen to the fear under 'AI will take my job'. Productive capacity and human security can move apart, so carry the gain through to the person.
We don't have to live like this: there is enough food, and scarcity is enforced by rules (eviction backed by a badge) that can change.
Money optional, not abolished; markets stay above the floor.
Renting survival is the design brief: produce it close to home, with neighbors.
One demonstration, seven days, three jobs, no villain. Good intentions don't govern a tool in other hands.

The book's definition: the Singularity is the point where intelligence stops being scarce and institutions built on its scarcity fail before replacements exist. No god required, and it is testable in your own paycheck. The emergency is the gap.
A dated, falsifiable forecast (AGI by Thanksgiving 2027) with the food work robust if it is wrong. Expert timelines moved earlier, and many researchers give real odds to catastrophe.
Plan by doors, not dates. Expert timelines are autopsies of the last failure (1903 Times versus the Wrights).
Four questions hide in one word: capability, improvement, deployment, access. This book lives in access.
Who gets the savings: the payroll incentive turns cheap thinking into hunger for specific people.
The near-term map: Stages 1 to 5 are scenarios, not a timetable. Stage 4, the new social contract, is the hinge and a choice we can start now.
Enclosure: you don't build anything, you build the fence. The builder finds he planted the hedge.
Exponentials look like nothing and then everything (star thistle). Seeing it coming exiles you from the people you love.
The threat was never man versus machine, it was man versus man.
Find the edge of your map and work the near end; a guess wearing a number's clothes is not knowledge.
Intelligence is energy, arranged. Physics checks claims but never prices a person, and somebody owns the meter.
Keep ledgers separate. Free at the point of access means paid for together, like a library.
When the cost per unit of work flips, sentiment doesn't save the incumbent (the horse and the ledger).
We are already inside it, but capability, deployment, ownership and access are separate. The gap is what we decide. Preservation solution: add abundance underneath everyone and take nothing.
Whose robots? Ownership has to reach the terms you depend on (Wiener 1949), because access can be withheld.
Technologies spread by group advantage, not consent, so spend energy on position, not 'whether'.
Reskilling is what the comfortable prescribe. Ask where the person stands while the transition happens (Denny).
The battle line is two reflexes, Entitled and Ready, that run through the same person. Fight for terms, not against the machine: build the floor Parliament wouldn't.
The floor is unconditional and must fit the person: Rosa owes no work day, and her dinner doesn't depend on the robots.
When intelligence is cheap, trust from specific people is the scarce asset. Work supplies more than pay, and scarcity narrows attention.
Argue about the machine's invoice, not its soul (the Music Performance Trust Fund).
Panic is a state, not information. Resilience comes from room to move, not attitude (Gary and Sal).
The cognitive firewall: no notifications, the 24-hour delay, batching, boredom on purpose.
Autonomy is relational: the lone bunker is a tomb. Start with three households, and never withhold food to keep people in line.
Design for repair. Shorten survival supply lines (deglobalization, not decentralization), plan at regional scale, and remember the controller isn't dinner.
Interdependence is efficiency in fair weather and contagion in foul (the Bronze Age tin).
Create more than you consume. A true story beats an optimized one, real experience is the scarce input, and the three judo rules follow.
Own the compute you think on. Knowing a system is not operating it: design so it survives one person's bad Friday.
Food first as a usable claim on the result. Follow one request all the way through before buying a machine.

Land is the input the machine can't make. A land trust runs enclosure in reverse, and trust closes what data can't. CT's core thesis: meet survival needs on your own ground or through a city that runs it better.
Help without condescension. The first infrastructure may be a phone somebody answers.
The shouse: production and shelter under one roof. Know your lane, never cut a load-bearing member first, and work with the building department.
Collapse is readable before it lands, so say so. Efficiency gains are choices about whose books show the loss, and security buys time to choose.
A meter tells the truth only where it sits, so know the ground's history. Distributed food production scales when someone organizes it (Victory Gardens).
Trust doesn't scale, blueprints do. Own your press; leverage is reach over permission.
A tool you can't understand, repair or run offline is a leash. Tools don't choose which future they serve, people do. Discipline is a practice, not a perimeter.
Premortem with names. Measure by the Adequate Level of Care. Build the machine and the promise together, and whoever automates answers for the people moved out.
The plan: survival as a public floor, built rung by rung, food first, with automation raising the floor. Each rung stands alone. Ask how a need became free somewhere else.
Civic action that works: a specific request sized to the speaking limit, followed up in writing. Testimony from the people affected beats the model.
One question for every automation decision: how will the people affected share in the benefit? The moral mandate. The last fence is inside you.
Bookend: the toast is reclaimed, the napkin redeemed, and the reader is holding the book.
The machine is unprecedented, the moment isn't. The Precedent Ledger device runs through each surviving chapter as story hook, mechanism and rule.
A year of small, sequenced actions: the single home for 'what do I do Monday'.

plan:zero.rationale: Zero to speed means a reader who has never thought about AI should be able to follow every chapter, care by the middle, and know what to do by the end. v0.11.0 fails that test as it stands. It runs 9,236 words of front matter (four front doors) before Chapter 1 says what the Singularity is, and it gives two conflicting AGI definitions. Part III spends thousands of words on reference material only a builder needs (VRAM, PID, nitrogen chemistry, mesh specs). Many chapters explain their own scenes after they land. So the book is not publishable as is for this reader. The core cut shows that its spine fits in about 50,000 words. The allocation follows the on-ramp. Front matter (Introduction, Preface, Chapter 0) gets 5,750, down from 9,236, and How to Use is dropped so the reader reaches the story quickly. Part I gets 9,662, weighted toward Chapter 1 (2,850, the definition, doors not dates, four questions and the payroll incentive), Chapter 2 (2,300, the Stage 1 to 5 map and the enclosure scene) and Chapter 5 (2,400, intelligence as energy, separate ledgers, the horse). The speculative Chapters 3 and 4 shrink to their scenes and hinge lines (2,050), with Stages 6 to 9 compressed in Appendix C. Part II gets 10,257 because it is where a newcomer starts to care and meets the core argument: capability versus access, the preservation solution, Denny's question, Rosa's floor, and the firewall that keeps a newly frightened reader from spiraling. Part III, Chapters 10 to 18, gets 17,115. Each chapter keeps its scene (the Elijah arc and the Conclusion's callbacks need them all) and the one principle a newcomer can act on, while the technical reference material goes. Chapter 19 and the Conclusion get 5,000, so the plan and the Bear Flag bookend survive nearly whole. Appendices get 2,060: Appendix G kept whole as the single sequenced action plan, Appendix A's nine questions because Chapter 19 points to them, and Appendix C cut to the objections list and the compressed stages. Appendices D, E, F and H are dropped because each duplicates kept chapters or would point at cut material; CT should regenerate the glossary and Ledger index in v0.12 from the final text. Where this angle will likely disagree with the others: a story-first architect may want more of Chapter 0's backstory and Chapters 3 and 4. A do-something architect may want more Part III how-to and the Appendix D symptom index. I traded those for definitions up front and for Chapters 6 to 8, because a newcomer who misses the definition or the floor argument cannot use the how-to. Budgets sum to 49,994, and no budget exceeds its file's total.

plan:path.thesis: Thinking machines are already cheap enough to run on a desk at home, and the old deal (sell your days or you don't eat) is failing faster than anyone is writing a replacement. CT forecasts AGI by Thanksgiving 2027, but nothing the book asks depends on the date. The real emergency is the gap between a dying labor-for-survival contract and the one nobody has written yet, and the reader can start closing it this week. Start with food: adequate food for everyone regardless of income or employment, as the first rung of a larger floor (land care, cleanup, shelter, care), with money made optional rather than abolished. Free at the door is not free to provide, so the work is building provision people can count on. That means tools you own and can repair, ground held together, small circles where nobody's meal depends on their share, and public institutions that turn the meal from charity into a service like the library. The reader leaves with a nine-rung ladder, a rung to stand on whoever they are, a year of concrete practices, and one question to bring to every automation decision. They also leave with the story of a man who went from handing strangers a telescope to handing a newcomer a broom. The shouse, the mesh and the cyberdeck are examples of one way among several, not the price of entry: you can take part without land, servers or a robot, including as the person receiving help.

spine.idea: The design brief: if machines can grow food and build houses, why am I still renting my survival? Build what makes the question obsolete, close to home, with neighbors, starting now.
We don't have to live like this: there is enough food; scarcity is an enforced arrangement of rules people wrote and can rewrite; money should be optional, not abolished.
Productive capacity and human security can diverge; a gain in producing should become a gain in living, and losing a job should stop threatening dinner.
Food first, not food only: adequate food for everyone regardless of income or employment, then land care, cleanup, shelter and care.
Free at the door is not free to provide: fund provision together the way we fund a library, name the maintenance, and start feeding people while arguing about funding.
Use the tools yourself; do not take the pundits' word or the author's.

The working definition: the Singularity is when intelligence stops being scarce and institutions built on that scarcity fail before a replacement exists; the emergency is the gap, and you can test it on your own paycheck this quarter.
Plan by doors, not dates: a bounded forecast, an asymmetric bet, a timeline file, and a first question to take to a grower before proposing any robot.
Stage 4 is a decision available now: the machine that can do the work doesn't write the terms; commit a share of capacity to food regardless of employment.
Work the near end: speculation turns the reader back to the human question of who gets fed, housed and decides.
Energy is the base layer: audit your inputs, leaks and pod; keep the ledgers separate; never let physics price a person; own one small machine.
The preservation solution and the ownership question: add dependable abundance under everyone, take nothing, and make sure ownership reaches the terms people depend on.

plan:path.rationale: The 50,047 words are weighted toward what a reader does after closing the book. Part III, Chapter 19 and the Conclusion take 24,498 words, about 49 percent. Chapter 19 gets the single largest budget (3,500), because the Introduction promises it as the step-by-step plan and its Who lines put every reader on a rung. Part II gets 9,557 words, because the floor, the invoice, the firewall, start with three, and design for repair are where the reader's habits change. Part I is compressed to 7,380: the definition, doors not dates, Stage 4 as a decision available now, the energy audit, and the narrative turn to 'Work the near end'. The Stage 7 to 9 speculation, the simulation trilemma, the lineage roll call and the Transformer lecture are dropped. The front matter keeps 5,612 words: the thesis and design brief, CT's April 2024 opening and horse parable, the routing table, and Chapter 0's cold open, which plants nearly every gun the Conclusion fires. The back matter is cut to 3,000 words of pure tools: Appendix G whole as the year plan, Appendix D's 24 rules as the Ledger's surviving form and the decoder for G's tags, Appendix A's organizer questions, Appendix C's hand-off page, and a slim Appendix E for Tier 0 and Tier 1. Appendices F and H are dropped as regenerable back matter. Across the book the cuts fall hardest on figures, captions, formulas, hedges, sourcing detail, duplicated arguments (the cook, food-first-not-only, the tools don't pick, free is not costless, mesh, land trusts, model collapse), and precedent stories whose rules already live in Appendix D. Elijah's arc is protected end to end: witness, apprentice with a broom, builder, county hearing, the book left on the bar. It is the book's model of a person who stopped watching and started doing, and cutting it would leave the call to action without the example that makes it believable. Every budget is within its file's total, and the plan leaves room for CT to make his own block choices inside each file.

plan:story.thesis: Machines can now do much of the thinking people are paid for, cheaply and soon, and the old deal (sell your days or don't eat) is ending before anyone has written its replacement. That gap is the real emergency, and it is a choice, not a law of physics: there is enough food, scarcity is enforced by rules people wrote, and we don't have to live like this. The answer the core keeps is concrete enough to start on Monday. Food comes first, for everyone, whatever their work or money. Money becomes optional, not abolished. Survival is produced close to home, on machines and land people own together, instead of rented from whoever owns the machines. The public floor is built rung by rung. The core carries that argument inside a story a newcomer can feel. Elijah, a farm kid who demos the future at a bar and helps end three careers, spends three years being corrected by a welder, a twice-reskilled warehouse worker, a soil scientist, a hardware man and a woman with a braced wrist. He learns that the answer to the machine was never a smarter machine. It was people who know each other, multiplied. The book has to end where it began, at the Bear Flag, with the toast reclaimed and the book left on the bar for the reader to pick up.

spine.idea: What is happening: thought itself is now automated, cheaply and on home hardware; the tool can now invent tools.

The Singularity defined as the point where intelligence stops being scarce and institutions built on that scarcity fail before a replacement exists, made concrete by CT's Einstein-as-tech-support picture and testable against your own paycheck.
A dated, falsifiable forecast (AGI by Thanksgiving 2027), with advice that holds even if the date is wrong.
Plan by doors, not dates: expert timelines are autopsies of the last failure, so make one asymmetric bet.
Make the machines grow our food first: adequate food for everyone, whatever their income or job, as the first rung of a larger project.
We don't have to live like this: there is enough food, and scarcity is enforced by rules people can change.
Productive capacity and human security can move in opposite directions; carry the gain through to the person.
The design brief: why am I still renting my survival? Produce it instead, close to home, with neighbors.
Money becomes optional, not abolished; markets stay above the floor.
Enclosure and complicity: the well-meaning builder discovers he built the fence; the land trust runs enclosure in reverse.
Stage 4 is the hinge: a machine that can do the work doesn't write the terms, and the decision can start now.
Intelligence is energy, arranged; physics never prices a person; keep the ledgers separate; free at the door means paid for together, like a library.
Capability is not access; the preservation solution adds abundance underneath people and takes nothing from anyone; who owns the robots decides who gets fed.
Reskilling versus the floor: where does a person stand while the transition happens? Build the floor Parliament wouldn't, unconditionally.
When intelligence is cheap, trust from specific people becomes the scarce asset; small circles have to keep adding chairs.
Resilience depends on conditions, not attitude; build a cognitive firewall; autonomy is relational, and a circle never withholds food to keep people in line.
Design for repair over elegance; deglobalize survival needs; plan at the scale of the region; map your tin.
Create more than you consume; real human experience is now the scarce input; wrap practical knowledge in a true story (algorithmic judo).
Knowing a system is not the same as operating it; design for the bad Friday, not for the careful person.
Land is the one input the machine can't make more of; meet survival needs on your own ground or through a city that runs that infrastructure better; trust closes what data can't.
Own the dirt, then build: the shouse, production and shelter under one roof, without a thirty-year mortgage.
If you see collapse coming, say so; efficiency is a choice about whose books show the loss; security buys time to choose.
A meter tells the truth only about where it sits; know the ground's history; distributed food production scales sideways when someone organizes it.
Trust doesn't scale; files do. Ship the blueprints and keep the trust local. Leverage is reach divided by permission.
A tool you can't understand, repair or run offline is a leash; discipline is a practice, not a perimeter.
The premortem with people in it, the Adequate Level of Care as the yardstick, and building the machine and the promise together; nobody should have to be liked to be fed.
The ladder: make survival a public floor instead of a private purchase, rung by rung, with testimony doing the work the model can't; ask who it can't be afforded by.
The moral mandate and the landing: you weren't born to increase shareholder value, and the answer to the machine was people who know each other, multiplied.

principles: Cut whole blocks only, verbatim. Never trim a sentence; when a kept block points at cut material, flag it for CT's v0.12 rewrite rather than patching it.
Scenes come first. Every Elijah and co-op scene keeps its load-bearing beats (about 23,000 of the 50,000 words), because the story is what carries a newcomer through the argument.

When the narrator or the author explains a beat that has already landed, cut the explanation (sts.chapter0.b0061, b0091, b0065; sts.chapter1.b0017, b0099 to b0101; sts.chapter2.b0124; sts.chapter4.b0082; sts.chapter18.b0145; sts.chapter19.b0093). The voice guide's rule is that a scene never announces its lesson.
A setup stays only if its payoff stays, and the reverse. If one of a pair cannot fit, both go. Check every planted gun against its firing block before dropping either.
One instance per idea. Keep the sharpest and earliest version in CT's voice, or the scene that dramatizes it, and cut the restatements. When a later chapter names the earlier one, keep the named one.

CT's voice beats committee voice. Keep the profanity that earns its place (sts.introduction.b0050, sts.introduction.b0148, sts.chapter12.b0136, sts.chapter13.b0164, sts.chapter19.b0096, sts.chapter19.b0105) and the hammer lines. Cut blocks whose only job is to hedge, disclaim or fact-check a claim the cut no longer makes.
Drop apparatus wholesale: figures, captions, epigraphs, In this chapter bullets, interactive markers, LaTeX and code. The only exception is an epigraph a character answers (sts.chapter17.b0151).

Keep a precedent's story when it is genuinely a story (the Wrights, Watt's horse, the orchestra-pit robot, the Bronze Age tin, the Victory Gardens, Paine, Y2K, the NHS). Drop precedents whose rule contradicts their own chapter (P-15, P-17), duplicate a scene (P-09), lean on a cut precedent (P-18), or are weak (P-01, P-05, P-14). P-24 goes so the moral mandate runs straight into the Bear Flag. Appendix D keeps all twenty-four rules in one line each.
Keep the speculative chapters for their scenes (the thistle, the mother's call, LADDER.xlsx) and cut their seminars (the simulation trilemma, Stage 7, Stage 9).
Keep one practice per chapter where it is the most usable action in the chapter, so the book still changes what a reader does this week without Appendix G.

Back matter that can be regenerated (the glossary, How to Use, the discussion guide, the year plan, the cyberdeck spec, the council brief) goes. Keep only the condensed handout (Appendix C) and the compressed Ledger (Appendix D).
Get to the hook faster. Keep the Introduction's hammer lines and the Preface's 2024 opener and horse parable. Cut the tours, routing, disclaimers and stat runs that bury them.
Never cut a block that a kept block names by chapter or by detail. Where that has already happened, list it as a seam for CT.
No em dashes or en dashes in anything the architects write. Dashes inside kept book text (the chapter titles of Ch2 to Ch4) are flagged for CT, not edited.
plan:story.rationale:
I built these budgets from a block-by-block keep list, not from tier ratios, so each number is the sum of a specific set of whole blocks I checked against the annotated files. That makes each budget a selection the next stage can reproduce. The total is 50,003 words; Appendix B is excluded.

Shape of the cut. About 23,000 words are scene. Chapter 0 keeps 83 percent (3,167) because it plants nearly every gun the Conclusion fires. The Bear Flag coda keeps all 903 of its words. Every co-op scene survives with its friction beat and its payoff. The remaining 27,000 are argument, precedent and back matter. Each spine idea appears once, in its sharpest and most CT-voiced form. The Introduction keeps 2,474 hammer-heavy words, and Chapter 19 keeps 2,843 (the scene, the rawest author voice, every rung's What line and two unique proofs).

Precedents. Sixteen chapter precedents survive, most of them compressed. Appendix D keeps all twenty-four rules, so the Ledger is still complete in one breath each.

Back matter. Appendices A, E, F, G and H and How to Use go, because each is either regenerable after v0.12 or a duplicate. Appendix C stays as the ten-minute handout, carrying the full nine-stage map now that the Stage 7 and Stage 9 Foundations are cut.

Biggest cuts by chapter. Ch11 keeps 41 percent: the Hansard history, the VRAM and heat math, the objections FAQ and P-14 go. Ch14 keeps 45 percent: P-17 and P-18 go because they argue against Frank. Ch17 keeps 46 percent: SECTOR 07 and the reference catalog go. Ch7 keeps 53 percent: P-09 and the letterhead table go, since Marta already told the Luddite story. Ch5 keeps 53 percent: the cyberdeck and Tiffany run goes; it duplicates P-01 and Appendix E and scolds older readers.

Verdict on publishing v0.11.0 as is: no. Story and voice are the book's strongest assets, and v0.11.0 buries them. The front matter runs 9,320 words of four front doors before Chapter 1, and CT's April 2024 first line sits at word 3,803. Nearly every scene is followed by narration explaining it. The Conclusion ends three times. Several precedents contradict their own chapters (P-15 and P-17), and the Introduction's AI-slop riff mocks the artists Chapter 0 grieves for. Every one of those can be fixed by cutting whole blocks, which is the evidence that a strong book sits inside this one.
